title: Epileptic seizures
blurb: Keep a fitting patient safe, time the seizure, and know when buccal midazolam and a 999 call are needed.
question: A patient with epilepsy suddenly goes stiff in the dental chair, cries out, then starts jerking. The dentist still has a mouth mirror in her mouth. What should you do in the first minute, and what would make this a seizure that needs midazolam?

teach.body: A seizure is a sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. The one you are most likely to manage is a tonic-clonic seizure: the patient loses consciousness, goes stiff, then jerks rhythmically. Most stop on their own within a few minutes. In the surgery, seizures can be set off by missed medication, missed meals, tiredness, stress or flickering lights. Low blood glucose can also cause a seizure, so think about it in diabetic patients.

items.label: Aura: a strange feeling, smell or taste (not always)
Stiffens, may cry out, breathing may pause, may go blue
Rhythmic jerking; may bite tongue or wet themselves

teach.h: During the seizure: do and don't

rows.label: Remove instruments from the mouth only if it is safe
Clear equipment away and cushion the head
Hold the patient down or restrain movements
Put anything in the mouth, including fingers
Give food or drink, or move them unless in danger

teach.note: If it happens in the dental chair, it's usually safest to leave the patient there, reclined and lowered, with the bracket table moved away.

steps.label: Stop treatment, note the time
steps.sub: Remove instruments if safe; call for help

steps.label: Protect from injury
steps.sub: Clear the area, cushion the head, don't restrain

steps.label: Stay with them
steps.sub: Until fully recovered; record what happened

teach.caption: Given only if a convulsive seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures recur in quick succession (SDCEP).

teach.body: Most seizures stop by themselves. One that lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures that follow one another without recovery in between, may not stop without treatment and can become status epilepticus, which is life-threatening and can damage the brain. Midazolam calms the brain's electrical activity. It is given buccally: gently squirted into the space between the gum and the cheek, where it is absorbed through the lining of the mouth. Some patients carry their own prefilled syringes and a care plan.

items.label: strength of the emergency kit midazolam

teach.text: Never put anything in a fitting patient's mouth (no fingers, props or 'tongue guards') and never hold them down: both cause injuries. Patients do not swallow their tongue. Remove loose instruments only if you can do it safely.

teach.body: Call 999 if the seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, if seizures repeat, if it is the patient's first ever seizure, if they are injured, have trouble breathing, or don't recover as expected. Once the jerking stops, check their breathing and place them in the recovery position. Expect a period of drowsiness and confusion. Stay with them, don't restart treatment, and make sure they are not sent home alone.

items: Tonic-clonic seizure: stiffening, then rhythmic jerking, then a drowsy post-ictal phase.
Note the time, protect from injury, don't restrain, nothing in the mouth.
Seizure 5 minutes or more, or repeated: buccal midazolam and call 999.
Adult buccal midazolam 10 mg (2 mL of 5 mg/mL) between gum and cheek.
After: check breathing, recovery position, oxygen, stay with them.

summary: You can now recognise the phases of a tonic-clonic seizure, keep the patient safe without restraining them, decide when a seizure needs buccal midazolam and a 999 call, give the right dose for the patient's age, and care for them as they recover.

A.q: A patient starts having a tonic-clonic seizure in the dental chair. What should you do first?
options: Hold her arms still to stop the jerking
Put a mouth prop between her teeth
Move instruments away and note the time
Give her a sugary drink straight away
A.why: The priority is preventing injury and timing the seizure, which decides whether midazolam is needed.

whyNot.0: Restraining a fitting patient can cause injuries such as fractures.
whyNot.1: Nothing should be put in the mouth during a seizure; it can break teeth or cause choking.
whyNot.3: Food or drink can't be swallowed safely during a seizure.

A.q: When should buccal midazolam be given for an epileptic seizure?
options: As soon as the jerking starts
Only once the patient wakes up
If it lasts 5 minutes or more
A.why: Midazolam is given only if a convulsive seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures recur in quick succession.

whyNot.0: Most seizures stop on their own within a few minutes, so it isn't given straight away.
whyNot.1: Once the patient has woken, the seizure is over and midazolam isn't needed.
whyNot.2: Short seizures that stop on their own don't need midazolam.

A.q: What is the adult dose of buccal midazolam for a prolonged seizure?
A.why: Adults receive 10 mg of buccal midazolam, which is 2 mL of the 5 mg/mL solution.

whyNot.0: 2.5 mg is the dose for an infant aged 6 to 11 months.
whyNot.1: 5 mg is the dose for a child aged 1 to 4 years.
whyNot.3: 20 mg is double the recommended adult dose.

B.why: Buccal means the cheek: the liquid is placed between the gum and the cheek, where it is absorbed through the lining.

whyNot.0: IM injection into the thigh is the route for adrenaline.
whyNot.2: Sprays under the tongue describe GTN for angina.
whyNot.3: A fitting patient can't swallow a tablet safely.

B.q: The jerking stops. The patient is breathing but drowsy and confused. What should you do?
options: Sit her up and carry on treatment
Give midazolam to stop a repeat
Send her home in a taxi alone
Put her in the recovery position
B.why: After a seizure, check breathing and place the patient in the recovery position to protect the airway while they recover.

whyNot.0: Treatment shouldn't restart; the patient needs time to recover.
whyNot.1: Midazolam isn't given once a seizure has stopped.
whyNot.2: A post-ictal patient is confused and mustn't be sent home alone.

B.q: Which is NOT correct during a tonic-clonic seizure?
B.why: The limbs should never be restrained; this can cause injury. Let the seizure run its course while protecting the patient.

whyNot.0: Cushioning the head is correct and prevents injury.
whyNot.1: Timing the seizure is correct; it tells you if midazolam is needed.
whyNot.3: Clearing equipment away is correct and prevents injury.

C.q: After a seizure, the patient is drowsy and confused for several minutes. What is this called?
options: The start of a second seizure
C.why: The post-ictal phase is the period of drowsiness and confusion after a seizure ends.

whyNot.1: The tonic phase is the stiffening at the start of the seizure.
whyNot.2: Drowsiness and confusion are expected recovery, not a new seizure.
whyNot.3: An aura is a warning feeling some patients get before a seizure.

C.q: In which situation should you call 999?
options: A known epileptic's brief seizure, fully recovered
A patient who reports a passing aura
A patient who forgot their medication
C.why: A first ever seizure always needs urgent medical assessment, as do seizures lasting 5 minutes or more or repeated seizures.

whyNot.0: A short seizure in a known epileptic with full recovery doesn't usually need an ambulance.
whyNot.2: An aura that passes without a seizure doesn't need 999, though the patient should be monitored.
whyNot.3: Forgetting medication is a risk to note, not an emergency in itself.

C.q: A 7-year-old's convulsive seizure has lasted 5 minutes. What dose of buccal midazolam is correct?
C.why: Children aged 5 to 9 receive 7.5 mg (1.5 mL of 5 mg/mL).

whyNot.0: 10 mg is the dose for adults and children aged 10 to 17.
whyNot.1: 2.5 mg is for infants aged 6 to 11 months.
whyNot.2: 5 mg is for children aged 1 to 4.

reteach.title: Your job: bodyguard and timekeeper
reteach.question: During a seizure you can't stop the fit. So what exactly is your job while it happens, and what changes once it ends?

blocks.body: While the patient is fitting you are a bodyguard: move hard things away, cushion the head, and let the movements happen. You are also the timekeeper: the clock tells you whether this is a seizure that will stop on its own or one that needs midazolam and an ambulance. When it ends, your job becomes protecting the airway while the patient sleeps it off.

explain.body: A tonic-clonic seizure: sudden loss of consciousness, stiffening (tonic), then rhythmic jerking (clonic), then drowsiness (post-ictal).

test.q: A patient loses consciousness, goes rigid, then starts rhythmic jerking of all limbs. What is happening?
test.why: Loss of consciousness with stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking is a tonic-clonic seizure.

whyNot.0: A faint is a brief, floppy collapse with quick recovery when flat.
whyNot.1: A stroke usually causes one-sided weakness and slurred speech.
whyNot.3: Asthma causes wheeze and breathlessness, not convulsions.

explain.body: Clear the area and cushion the head. Never restrain or put anything in the mouth. Leave the patient where they are unless they are in danger.

test.q: A colleague reaches to put a wad of gauze between a fitting patient's teeth 'to protect the tongue'. What should you say?
options: Good idea, it stops tongue biting
Use a mouth prop instead of gauze
Nothing should go in the mouth
Only do it once the jerking slows
test.why: Nothing should be placed in the mouth during a seizure; it can break teeth, injure the rescuer or block the airway.

whyNot.0: The risk of injury and choking outweighs any benefit.
whyNot.1: A mouth prop is just as dangerous.
whyNot.3: It is unsafe at any stage of the seizure.

explain.body: If a convulsive seizure lasts 5 minutes or more, or seizures repeat, give buccal midazolam between the gum and cheek and call 999. Adult dose 10 mg (2 mL of 5 mg/mL).

test.q: A seizure started at 10:02. At what point should buccal midazolam be given if it hasn't stopped?
test.why: Midazolam is given once a convulsive seizure has lasted 5 minutes: 10:07 here.

whyNot.0: One minute is too soon; most seizures stop on their own.

explain.body: Check breathing, place in the recovery position and give oxygen. Stay with the patient until fully recovered. Call 999 for a first seizure, a seizure of 5 minutes or more, repeated seizures, injury or poor recovery.

test.q: Once a seizure ends and the patient is breathing, why are they placed in the recovery position?
test.why: The recovery position lets saliva or vomit drain and keeps the tongue from blocking the airway of a drowsy patient.

whyNot.2: Raising the legs, not the recovery position, helps blood pressure in a faint.
whyNot.3: It protects the airway; it doesn't make them wake faster.
